articleTitle: Some system considerations for electronic countermeasures to synthetic aperture radar
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The SEASAT mission of 1978 demonstrated the potential effectiveness of space-based synthetic aperture radar (SAR) for maritime reconnaissance. However, a significant vulnerability to electronic countermeasures can be shown to exist for SAR, which will tend to nullify this potential. Some critical systems aspects, in terms of jammer receiver sensitivity and transmitter power, for simple spot-noise jamming of a typical space-based SAR are considered and the systems requirements derived to determine the feasibility and practicality of such jamming. Finally, results of computer simulation of an engagement between the SAR and a representative jammer system are given to enable the effectiveness of the electronic countermeasures to be assessed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of radar environment simulation for operator training and EW system test and evaluation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: Radar environment simulation techniques are required to subject automatic ESM (electronic support measure) systems and their operators to real time test scenarios which would otherwise only be available during expensive trials. Simulators may be used to verify the integrity of system antennas, receivers, processing algorithms and interfaces, as well as to train operators, The type of simulator selected will depend on which part of the ESM system is to be exercised. The author describes the simulation functions and the interfacing to the system under test by way of digital simulation, video simulation, injected RF simulation and radiated RF simulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of neural networks to radar classification
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The authors investigate the temporal and spectral features from a variety of different (but similar) radars using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifier. This nonlinear neural network (NN), trained using error back-propagation, has been shown to be able to classify these different radars with a reasonably low probability of error. Additionally an attempt was made to interpret the NN as a (fast) digital filter structure so that it could be readily implemented in discrete technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An analysis of the performance of DRFMS for EW systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The effects of systematic errors in a coherent I/Q circuit with digital detectors on frequency accuracy have been analysed and measured. An expression has been derived for the RMS accuracy of frequency measurement for ADCs with a given number of effective bits (N/sub ef/). No account has been taken of random noise on the signal and this may account for calibration not restoring maximum performance. The discrepancy is greatest at lowest and highest frequencies. At low frequencies, one channel provides consistently better N/sub ef/ than the other whereas the analysis assumes equal performance. Also, SNR/sub act/ has fallen from 34.5 dB at 10 MHz to 21.0 dB at 180 MHz and this may explain why calibration provides no benefit at high frequencies. It has been shown that a further improvement in accuracy may be obtained by a linear trade-off with bandwidth.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer modelling of advanced radar techniques: the Advanced Radar Simulator
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: Engineers regularly use computer models to simulate the systems they design. However, due to the complexity of the processing required, most of these models have been limited to small scale simulations. The increased availability of high powered computers over recent years has greatly improved this situation. The author describes the Advanced Radar Simulator, a detailed computer model developed by Thorn EMI Electronics to model large scale radar scenarios. The design philosophy behind the model is explained, with particular reference to the importance of ensuring that the model's structure and operation accurately represents real physics processes. Some examples of its use are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Unambiguous frequency measurement in a scanning superheterodyne receiver
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: Frequency is the single most important measurement for signal sorting and emitter identification in electronic support measures (ESM) receivers. There are a variety of techniques for making frequency measurements on radar signals. The authors describe a low-cost technique which may be applied to a scanning superheterodyne receiver. The technique has become applicable to ESM receivers as a result of developments in fast tuning, broadband voltage controlled oscillators (VCO) and has been demonstrated in a receiver covering a 3 to 1 bandwidth.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The AAETD: development of modular ESM systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: A study is being conducted on behalf of Missile Technology and Countermeasures (MTC3), Royal Aerospace Establishment, into the feasibility of an Advanced Airborne Electronic Warfare Technology Demonstrator (AAETD). This facility would provide a focus for the development of techniques and technologies for non-communications ESM (electronic support measures) systems. Support is planned for Tactical Surveillance Receiver (TSR), Radar Warning Receiver (RWR) and Anti-Radar Homing Receiver (ARHR) modes of operation. The AAETD will comprise both airborne and laboratory facilities. The authors describe the design philosophy, scope of the AAETD programme and present a feasibility study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The development of an ESM data processing scheme based on pattern recognition techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The author reports on a study to develop and test a novel scheme, called PREPS, based on pattern recognition techniques, for ESM data processing. The philosophy behind PREPS has been to process on a pulse-by-pulse basis and to make maximum use of intra-pulse parameters, using time of arrival only as a second stage parameter. The aim has been to design PREPS so that new pulse parameters can easily be utilised when they become available. A further design goal was to allow all stages of the processing to have access to all levels of data; thus, for example, an emitter can be analysed at any level down to its constituent pulses.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation of modern electronic combat scenarios by means of a flexible generic computer model
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The effectiveness of EW equipment and tactics is becoming more difficult to predict as the level of complexity of ECCM and ECM increases. Simulation, when validated, is an important tool in the evaluation of EW equipment and tactics. It complements traditional methods such as laboratory measurements or trials, providing a cost effective, secure and repeatable means of extrapolating into dense scenarios, performing sensitivity analysis, rapid prototyping of proposed enhancements, quantitative comparisons of alternative designs, and performance evaluation against current or postulated threats. To be most cost-effective, a tool should be flexible. A generic simulation model, with parametric functional models of equipment, provides maximum flexibility if it is based on a framework which imposes no unnecessary limitations. The requirements for such a framework have been given and an implementation of a pulse-by-pulse functional model by Software Sciences outlined. Sample applications of this model and others in the family have been given to demonstrate the simulation of modern electronic combat scenarios by means of a flexible generic computer model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High level modelling tools for tactical ELINT systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Warfare Systems
abstract: The author describes the modelling and analysis of ground-based tactical electronic intelligence (ELINT) systems, tasked with detecting and locating elements of a ground-based array of target radars. A representative tactical ELINT system consists of a baseline of two or more ground-based ESM sensors, having one or more broadband antennas and receivers. EAch sensor measures the bearing to a target radar, and reports that line of bearing to a control station which determines the emitter location by triangulation. The radars to be detected are described principally by their frequency and effective radiated power (ERP) in dBW: the detection process at the sensor is modelled simply by specifying a threshold incident power flux.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
